fixes.explanation: Yes, baker. God's word says that if they return to Him and keep His commandments, then even if the exiles are banished "…to the farthest horizon, I will gather them from there and bring them to the place I have chosen as a dwelling for My Name." (Nehemiah 1:9) That's a promise of gathering, no matter how far they've been scattered. Nehemiah brings that word up in his prayer, asking God to remember what He told Moses. (Nehemiah 1:8)
Nope, no army talk and no road directions here, friend. Nehemiah asks about the Jews who survived the exile and about Jerusalem. (Nehemiah 1:2) His questions are about people and a city.
Right, baker. The men say, "The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates have been burned with fire." (Nehemiah 1:3) The wall is down and the gates are burned. That's the news Nehemiah gets.

It's true, friend. Nehemiah says, "When I heard these words, I sat down and wept." (Nehemiah 1:4) He doesn't shrug it off or just nod politely. The news about Jerusalem's wall and gates brings him to tears.

Careful, baker, that's not what he says. Nehemiah calls God the one "…who keeps His covenant of loving devotion with those who love Him and keep His commandments…" (Nehemiah 1:5) He never says it's with every nation on earth. It's with those who love God and keep His commandments.
That's right, baker. Nehemiah says, "Both I and my father’s house have sinned." (Nehemiah 1:6) He confesses the sins the Israelites have committed, and he counts himself and his father's house in it.
That's the word, baker. Nehemiah prays, "…grant him mercy in the sight of this man." (Nehemiah 1:11) He's asking God for mercy in the sight of a man. He also asks God to give him success that day.

Reasonable guess, friend, but that's not the word in the verse. Nehemiah prays, "…grant him mercy in the sight of this man." (Nehemiah 1:11) He asks for mercy, not protection. He also asks God to give him success that day.
That's it, baker. Nehemiah adds, "(At that time I was the cupbearer to the king.)" (Nehemiah 1:11) He tucks it in at the very end, like a little footnote after the prayer.
I wish, friend, because I'd have stood up and cheered for a chief baker. But Nehemiah says, "At that time I was the cupbearer to the king." (Nehemiah 1:11) A cupbearer, not a baker.
Good guess, friend, but that's not the job Nehemiah names. He says, "At that time I was the cupbearer to the king." (Nehemiah 1:11) That's his job, and he mentions it right at the end of his prayer.
